cells.tense: You're here at the bench, and the work is moving — you can feel it, and you're not forcing it.
cells.ask: Name what the last finished piece taught you, then let the next one start from that instead of from the plan.
cells.core:
Your practice is steady and it's yours. You show up to the same small work most days, and the showing up has become a way of knowing — the hands remember what the mind hasn't worked out yet. Because you've let each round of work actually finish in you, the next idea arrives already part of you, not borrowed from somewhere. You can move through the unclear stretch without having to see the whole road.

What comes next is drive — not more force, but direction that comes from feeling. The work you've done is asking to be aimed somewhere. You can pick a direction today and keep it, and that pick will give the practice a spine it doesn't have when it's only repetition. Nothing huge — one decision about what the next season of this is for.
cells.sheetLine: Your practice has become a way of knowing, and it's ready to be aimed.
cells.verb: moving through uncertainty without forcing it clear
cells.place: at the bench, in the small daily practice

cells.tense: You're already living in the version of this that hasn't happened yet, and the practice has become a rehearsal for a future you can't write in.
cells.ask: Pick one finished thing and leave it alone for a day — don't refine it, don't plan its next stage, just let it sit.
cells.core:
The practice is a small steady light — you keep it lit by attention, and the light is enough to see the next step. The work grows on its own schedule and you tend it without forcing.

Lately the light has flooded the room. You're refining toward a picture of what this will become, and the picture has more pull than the work in front of you. Each session is spent making the real thing match the imagined one, and the gap doesn't close because you keep moving the target ahead of yourself. The work can't catch up. What might be underneath is that the imagined version is safe — it can't fail yet — while the finished thing can. The way back is care for what's actually growing: letting it be where it is, not where you've decided it should be. Leave one piece alone today and see if it holds up without your hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're refining toward a picture instead of tending what's here.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you — you decided, long before now, not to trust the unclear part, and the practice has been literal ever since.
cells.ask: Do one session with no plan and no goal — just make the first mark and follow it, and notice what guides your hand before you decide anything.
cells.core:
What this looks like when it's alive is simple: you show up, you do the work, and the work tells you something new. The small light is enough, and you trust it.

Lately the practice has gone flat — you want the steps and the instructions, and anything that arrives without a reason gets set aside. The depth is there and you've stopped reaching for it. This isn't laziness; it may be that trusting a direction you can't justify felt like a risk you didn't want to take. The way back is knowing what to attend to before you can explain why. Make one thing today without a plan, and let what you notice guide your hand. You don't have to argue for it, only follow it.
cells.sheetLine: The depth is there, and you've stopped trusting it.

cells.tense: You're writing in a room you're already in, but the pen is down — the imagining that shapes your work is running without your hand on it.
cells.ask: Before your next session, finish this one sentence on paper: 'The thing I keep making is really about ___.' Then close the notebook and do the practice as usual.
cells.core:
When this is working, the practice and the vision are one thing. You sit down, the work happens, and afterwards you can say what it was for. Solitude connects here; it doesn't isolate. Refinement serves the work instead of feeding worry.

Lately the practice is doing something you haven't claimed. The themes you're drawn to, the shapes that keep coming back — they're steering the work, and you'd describe the whole thing as just showing up and doing the exercises. The imagining is active; nobody's name is on it. The way back is practice that flows without force. One sentence, before the next session, naming what the work is really about. That's enough to put your hand back on the wheel. Nothing changes about the practice — only about who's holding it.
cells.sheetLine: The work is steering itself, and you haven't claimed the wheel.
cells.verb: moving through uncertainty without forcing it clear
cells.place: at the bench, in the small daily practice

attempts.check: The draft claims the person's solitude is already shaping what they make, which the record supports only as a capacity in this seat, not as a fact about their life; a reader could say the imagination is obvious and deliberate, not unnoticed. The ask (one session of practice, watch what the work does before you touch it) is still useful if the read is wrong, because it teaches them something about how they relate to their own craft regardless. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any line about 'what you're already dreaming' — it sounds like a verdict on their life rather than a description of a capacity, so I've kept it tied to the work itself.
